title: Cobalt Basin: why did profit fall in a record snow season?
prompt: Cobalt Basin is an independent ski resort in the US Rocky Mountains. This winter it had record snowfall and more skier visits than ever, yet its profit halved, from $20 million to $10 million. The CEO wants to know why, and what to do before next season. How would you approach this?

facts.answer: Cobalt Basin owns its lifts, ski school, rental shops and restaurants. It does not own any hotels; lodging nearby is run by other companies. It is about two hours' drive from a large city.
The CEO wants profit back to at least $20 million next season, without cutting safety or the quality of the slopes.
Snowfall was the highest on record and conditions were excellent all season. The season was the usual length.

Day-ticket prices did not change, at about $100 per visit on average. Last spring the resort cut the season pass price from $800 to $400 to build loyalty and sell more passes before the season. Data on visits and passes is available.

Day-ticket visitors mostly come from the city or from other states, and many rent equipment or take lessons. Pass holders are mostly locals and city regulars who own their gear. A pass holder skis about 10 days a season.
Day-ticket visitors spend about $50 per visit on food, rentals and lessons. Pass holders spend about $20 per visit.

Staff costs are mostly fixed for the season. Snow operations (grooming, clearing parking lots and avalanche control) rose with the record snow. Other costs did not change. A profit and loss by season is available.
On peak weekends and holidays the lift lines were long and the parking lots were full by 9am. Some day-ticket visitors were turned away or went to other resorts.
Two larger resorts nearby kept their season passes at about $900 and their day tickets at about $110.
Nobody can forecast it. Assume a normal snow year for planning.

key_buckets: Lift revenue: visits by type (day ticket or season pass) x lift revenue per visit
Revenue from extras: food, rentals and lessons per visit, by type of visitor
Costs: staff, snow operations and other costs, this season versus last
What changed: weather, prices, the pass and the visitor mix, crowding
Fixes for next season and their effect on profit
good_signs: Notices the puzzle: visits rose but profit fell, so revenue per visit or costs must explain it
Separates one-off weather effects from lasting effects of the resort's own decisions
Segments visitors into day-ticket buyers and pass holders
Quantifies each driver's share of the fall
red_flags: Blames the weather without checking revenue
Suggests cutting staff or slope quality without evidence

exhibits.title: Cobalt Basin profit and loss by season ($ million)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask for revenue and costs by line, this season versus last.
exhibits.insight: Profit fell $10 million. Revenue fell $7 million (lift tickets and passes down $6 million, extras down $1 million) even though visits rose, and snow operations rose $3 million. Lower revenue explains 70% of the fall; the snow costs only 30%.

exhibits.title: Visits and season passes by season
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask how visits, ticket types or pass sales changed, or why lift revenue fell when visits rose.
exhibits.insight: Total visits rose 20%, but all the growth was pass visits (from 100,000 to 300,000) while day-ticket visits fell by 100,000. Halving the pass price meant it paid for itself after 4 days instead of 8, so many day-ticket buyers switched. Lift revenue per visit fell from $96 to $70.

math.question: What was lift revenue per visit this season, in dollars?
math.working: $42 million / 600,000 visits = $70 per visit, down from $96 last season ($48 million / 500,000 visits).

math.question: Using the spending per visit for each type of visitor, how much did the resort make from food, rentals and lessons this season, in $ million?
math.working: Day-ticket visitors: 300,000 x $50 = $15 million. Pass holders: 30,000 passes x 10 visits = 300,000 visits x $20 = $6 million. Total $21 million, $1 million less than last season despite 100,000 more visits.

math.question: What percentage of the $10 million fall in profit comes from lower revenue?
math.working: Lift revenue fell $6 million and extras $1 million: $7 million of the $10 million fall, or 70%. The other 30% is the $3 million rise in snow operations, which should not repeat in a normal winter.

math.question: With this season's 30,000 passes and 300,000 day-ticket visits, what season pass price would have kept lift revenue at last season's $48 million, in dollars?
math.working: Day tickets brought in 300,000 x $100 = $30 million. The gap to $48 million is $18 million. $18 million / 30,000 passes = $600 per pass.

brainstorm.question: How could Cobalt Basin bring profit back to at least $20 million next season?
idea_bank: Raise the season pass price to about $600, still well below rivals' $900, with an early-bird discount
Offer tiers: a cheaper midweek-only pass and a full pass that costs more
Add blackout dates on peak weekends and holidays to the cheaper passes
Cap the number of season passes sold
Use dynamic day-ticket prices: higher on peak days, cheaper midweek and when bought in advance
Introduce reservations or paid parking on peak days to manage crowding
Sell extras to pass holders, such as lesson packs, prepaid food cards and lockers
Win back day visitors with bus packages from the city and midweek group and school deals
Add summer activities such as mountain biking and hiking so the lifts earn money all year
Plan snow operations better, for example with fuel contracts and grooming schedules, to soften costs in heavy snow years

must_mention: Profit halved mainly because of the pass price cut: lower lift and extras revenue explain $7 million (70%) of the $10 million fall, while one-off snow costs explain $3 million (30%)
The cheap pass moved day-ticket buyers onto passes, so lift revenue per visit fell from $96 to $70
Reprice the pass: about $600 would have kept lift revenue at $48 million, and tiered or blackout-date passes protect peak days for day-ticket buyers
good_signs: Checks the target: with lift revenue back at $48 million, extras at about $21 million and normal snow costs, profit would be about $19 million, so winning back day visitors closes the rest
Names the risks: pass holders may react badly to a 50% increase, and rivals may respond
Proposes what to track, such as spring pass sales and day-ticket visits on peak days

model_answer_outline: Clarify: profit fell from $20 million to $10 million in a record snow season with more visits. The goal is at least $20 million next season. Day-ticket prices did not change, but the pass price was cut from $800 to $400.

Structure: profit = revenue - costs. Revenue = visits by type x (lift revenue per visit + extras per visit). Costs split into staff, snow operations and other. Then ask what changed: the weather or the resort's own decisions.
Diagnosis: revenue fell $7 million (lift tickets and passes $6 million, extras $1 million) and snow operations rose $3 million, so lower revenue is 70% of the fall.

Root cause: passes tripled to 30,000 at half the price, and day-ticket visits fell from 400,000 to 300,000. Lift revenue per visit fell from $96 to $70, and pass holders spend $20 on extras against $50 for day visitors. Crowding on peak days pushed away more day visitors.
Math: a pass price of about $600 would have kept lift revenue at $48 million at this season's volumes. With normal snow costs, profit would then be about $19 million.

Recommendation: reprice the pass to about $600 (still well below rivals' $900), add a cheaper midweek-only pass and blackout dates on peak days, use dynamic day-ticket prices, and sell extras to pass holders. Track spring pass sales and day-ticket visits on peak days.
